title: M100 WFC3
caption: Spiral galaxy M100, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: Location not published by the source

recognition.text: NASA Hubble image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: Two prominent lanes of young, blue stars sweep around the spiral galaxy M100, while its inner region glows yellowish with older populations of stars. Closer in, two tightly wound spiral arms wrap around the core, where a small bar of stars sits. M100 is a grand-design spiral, a name given to galaxies with well-defined, prominent arms.
The arms trace ripples of matter moving through the galaxy's disc of stars. Where they pass, gas piles up into denser regions, and those denser areas trigger new star formation.

Hubble took this picture with Wide Field Camera 3, installed by astronauts on the last space shuttle servicing mission in May 2009, a few months before the photo. M100 holds a special place in Hubble history. In 1993, while NASA prepared to correct a manufacturing flaw in Hubble's main mirror, it was picked as a target to show the planned fix. A blurry picture was taken before the repair, and after the December 1993 servicing mission the galaxy snapped into sharp focus.
scale: M100 lies 55 million light-years away, according to NASA.

understand.summary: Taken with Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3. The color mapping is not published.
understand.eye: The picture combines separate filter images, and NASA does not say how the colors were assigned, so they need not match what an eye would see.

explore: NASA released this image to mark the 25th anniversary of the first astronaut servicing mission. M100 was chosen in 1993 partly because it would just fit inside Hubble's field of view. The blurry 1993 view came from the Wide Field and Planetary Camera 1, which astronauts swapped for the vision-corrected Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2.
sources: NASA release: Celebratory Galaxy Photo Honors 25th Anniversary of NASA’s First Hubble Servicing Mission
